work: Enarratio in Epistolam I B. Petri
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: ENARRATIO CAPITULI PRIMI : PETRUS APOSTOLUS JESU CHRISTI.
1.title_en: Explanation of the first chapter: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ.

paras.t: Petrus apostolus Jesu Christi. Quamvis princeps pastorum, Unigenitus Dei Jesus Christus, increata et æterna sapientia Dei Patris, gloriosissimum Petrum toti et universali prætulerit militanti Ecclesiæ, plenum, summum ac generalem suum vicarium constituens eum in terra, dicendo, Pasce oves meas; nihilo minus dicitur sacratissimus Petrus specialiter Judæorum fuisse apostolus, juxta illud ad Galatas: Qui operatus est Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est et mihi inter gentes. Quemadmodum enim Jacobus constitutus est Jerosolymitanorum Christianorum primus episcopus; sic Petrus omnium in Judæa, Samaria, Galilæa ac alibi, Judæorum instructioni, conversioni, gubernationi fuit specialiter desuper deputatus atque intentus. Hinc, ut apostolatus sui officium digne prosequeretur, duas conversis Judæis scripsit epistolas.
paras.en: [[1:1|Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ|Petrus apostolus Jesu Christi]]. Although the prince of pastors, the Only-begotten of God, Jesus Christ, the uncreated and eternal wisdom of God the Father, set the most glorious Peter over the whole and universal Church militant, making him his full, supreme and general vicar on earth when he said, [[John 21:17|Feed my sheep|Pasce oves meas]], nonetheless the most holy Peter is said to have been in a special way the apostle of the Jews, according to that word to the Galatians: [[Gal 2:8|he who wrought in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision wrought in me also among the Gentiles|Qui operatus est Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est et mihi inter gentes]]. For just as James was made the first bishop of the Christians of Jerusalem, so Peter was in a special way appointed from above to the instruction, conversion and government of all the Jews in Judea, Samaria, Galilee and elsewhere, and was intent upon it. Hence, so as to carry out the office of his apostleship worthily, he wrote two epistles to the converted Jews.

paras.t: Itaque in primæ suæ epistolæ ait exordio: Petrus apostolus Jesu Christi. Porro, in exordio secundæ suæ epistolæ ait: Simon Petrus. Cur ergo non exprimit nomen suum utrumque in principio hujus epistolæ, quemadmodum in illius? Et cur in utriusque initio vocat se Petrum magis quam Simonem? An forsan quia hoc nomen, Petrus, dulcius sapuit sibi, et magis gloriabatur de illo in Domino, eo quod Dominus Christus illud proprio sibi imposuerit ore, Tu es, inquiens, Petrus? Tamen, ut in Marco legitur, hoc nomen imposuit ei Christus in monte, quando ordinavit duodecim Apostolos. Denique, quum Petrus princeps Apostolorum esset, hoc humilitatis fuit quod se simpliciter nominavit apostolum.
paras.en: So at the opening of his first epistle he says: [[1:1|Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ|Petrus apostolus Jesu Christi]]. But at the opening of his second epistle he says: [[2 Pet 1:1|Simon Peter|Simon Petrus]]. Why then does he not give both his names at the beginning of this epistle, as he does at the beginning of that one? And why at the beginning of both does he call himself Peter rather than Simon? Is it perhaps because this name, Peter, was sweeter to his taste, and he gloried in it the more in the Lord, because the Lord Christ gave it him with his own mouth, saying, [[Matt 16:18|thou art|Tu es]], [[Matt 16:18|Peter|Petrus]]? Yet, as we read in Mark, Christ gave him this name on the mountain, when he ordained the twelve Apostles[[Mark 3:16||]]. Lastly, though Peter was the prince of the Apostles, it was a mark of humility that he named himself simply an apostle.

paras.t: Itaque, Petrus Christi apostolus scribit electis advenis. Secundum Bedam, advenæ Latine, Græce dicuntur proselyti: quo nomine appellabant Judæi eos qui ex gentilitate ad Judaismum erant conversi, sicut jam nuncupantur neophyti, qui infidelitate relicta, ad Christianismum convertuntur. De illorum autem advenarum seu proselytorum numero fuerunt nonnulli, qui in die sacratissimo Pentecostes, Petro prædicante, crediderunt in Christum, juxta illud Actuum: Judæi quoque et proselyti. His ergo, secundum Bedam, scripsit Petrus ambas suas epistolas: quod etiam Glossa ac alii protestantur.
paras.en: So Peter, the apostle of Christ, writes [[1:1|to the strangers|advenis]] who are [[1:1|elect|electis]]. According to Bede, those called *advenæ* [strangers, newcomers] in Latin are called proselytes in Greek: by this name the Jews called those who had been converted from heathenism to Judaism, as those who leave unbelief and are converted to Christianity are now called neophytes. Of the number of these strangers or proselytes were some who believed in Christ on the most holy day of Pentecost, when Peter preached, according to that word of the Acts: [[Acts 2:11|Jews also, and proselytes|Judæi quoque et proselyti]] [the margin's verse number is unreadable (Act. xi, …); the words are Acts 2:11]. To these, then, according to Bede, Peter wrote both his epistles; and the Gloss and others declare the same.

paras.t: Veruntamen verius reor, quod non eis dumtaxat, sed Judæis universis ad Christum conversis scripsit, quemadmodum Jacobus, sive ante susceptionem Judaismi fuerunt gentiles, sive non. Omnium namque generaliter habuit curam, caritatem et prælationem. Indigueruntque omnes exhortatione, instructione et consolatione summi Apostoli. Denique advenæ non solum dicuntur proselyti, quum primo Paralipomenon sanctus David loquatur ad Dominum: Peregrini sumus coram te et advenæ, sicut omnes patres nostri. Et Psalmista: Ne sileas, inquit, quoniam advena ego sum apud te. Omnes etenim Christiani viatores et advenæ vocantur, quia ad veram et cœlestem atque perpetuam patriam tendunt, et in sæculo isto, tanquam in exsilio, in terra aliena, in via, lacrimarumque valle degunt, prout ad Hebræos loquitur Paulus de veteribus Sanctis: Juxta fidem defuncti sunt omnes isti, non acceptis repromissionibus, sed eas a longe adspicientes et salutantes, et confitentes quia peregrini et hospites sunt super terram: qui enim hæc dicunt, significant se patriam inquirere.
paras.en: Yet I think it truer that he wrote not to them only, but to all the Jews converted to Christ, as James did, whether they had been Gentiles before they took up Judaism or not. For he had the care, the charity and the governance of all of them in general; and all of them needed the exhortation, instruction and consolation of the chief Apostle. Moreover, it is not only proselytes who are called strangers, since in the first book of Paralipomenon holy David says to the Lord: [[1 Par 29:15|we are sojourners before thee, and strangers, as were all our fathers|Peregrini sumus coram te et advenæ, sicut omnes patres nostri]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 38:13|Be no silent|Ne sileas]], he says, [[Ps 38:13|for I am a stranger with thee|quoniam advena ego sum apud te]]. For all Christians are called wayfarers and strangers, because they are making for the true, heavenly and everlasting fatherland, and in this world they live as in exile, in a strange land, on the road and in the valley of tears; as Paul says to the Hebrews of the holy men of old: [[Heb 11:13|All these died according to faith, not having received the promises but beholding them afar off and saluting them and confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth|Juxta fidem defuncti sunt omnes isti, non acceptis repromissionibus, sed eas a longe adspicientes et salutantes, et confitentes quia peregrini et hospites sunt super terram]]: [[Heb 11:14|they that say these things do signify that they seek a country|qui enim hæc dicunt, significant se patriam inquirere]].

paras.t: Igitur, juxta hanc advenæ significationem, sanctissimus princeps apostolici ordinis, universos ex Judaismo ad Christum conversos, vocat advenas, id est in sæculo isto peregrinos, viatores et exsules, juxta illud ad Hebræos: Non habemus hic manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus. Et recte sic nominat eos, ut implicite commoneat eos, non, juxta consuetudinem legis Mosaicæ, terrena bona, sed cœlestia præmia exspectare, appetere, atque accedere. Vocat quoque eos electos advenas, quia præ ceteris ad evangelicæ legis fidem et gratiam erant divinitus præordinati, vocati, perducti. Erant siquidem de electis illis reliquiis, de quibus Isaias prædixit: Si fuerit numerus filiorum Israel quasi arena maris, reliquiæ ex eis salvæ fient. De quibus ad Romanos inter cetera dicitur: Reliquiæ secundum electionem gratiæ Dei salvæ factæ sunt.
paras.en: So, in this sense of *stranger*, the most holy prince of the apostolic order calls all who were converted from Judaism to Christ [[1:1|strangers|advenas]], that is, pilgrims, wayfarers and exiles in this world, according to that word to the Hebrews: [[Heb 13:14|we have not here a lasting city: but we seek one that is to come|Non habemus hic manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus]]. And rightly does he name them so, to remind them by implication to look for, long for and draw near to heavenly rewards, not earthly goods as the custom of the law of Moses was. He also calls them [[1:1|elect|electos]] strangers, because beyond others they had been foreordained, called and brought by God to the faith and grace of the law of the Gospel. For they were of that chosen remnant of which Isaias foretold: [[Is 10:22|if thy people, O Israel, shall be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them|Si fuerit numerus filiorum Israel quasi arena maris, reliquiæ ex eis]] [[Is 10:22|shall be converted|salvæ fient]] [Denis's wording, *a remnant of them shall be saved*, is that of the quotation in Rom 9:27]. Of these it is said among other things to the Romans: [[Rom 11:5|a remnant saved according to the election of grace|Reliquiæ secundum electionem gratiæ Dei salvæ factæ sunt]].

paras.t: Itaque, Electis advenis dispersionis Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappadociæ, Asiæ et Bithyniæ, id est disgregationis factæ per regiones hic nominatas, quæ pertinebant ad Græciam, secundum Bedam et Glossam. Judæi quippe extra fines propriæ terræ erant per totum mundum dispersi: quorum multi in præfatis provinciis, scilicet Ponto, Galatia, etc., habitabant, et quidam eorum ad tempus in Jerusalem morabantur. Quumque credidissent, tandem a Judæis incredulis sunt expulsi, Stephano lapidato, ut legitur in Actibus.
paras.en: So: [[1:1|to the strangers dispersed through Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, elect|Electis advenis dispersionis Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappadociæ, Asiæ et Bithyniæ]] [the Douay-Rheims text in the app leaves out Galatia, which Denis reads], that is, of the scattering made through the regions here named, which belonged to Greece, according to Bede and the Gloss. For the Jews were scattered beyond the borders of their own land through the whole world; many of them lived in the provinces named, that is, Pontus, Galatia and so on, and some of them were staying for a time in Jerusalem. And when they had believed, they were at length driven out by the unbelieving Jews, after Stephen was stoned, as we read in the Acts[[Acts 8:1||]].

paras.t: Porro quod sequitur, secundum præscientiam Dei Patris, refertur ad illud, Electis advenis: quia electi fuerunt secundum præscientiam, id est prædestinationem, Dei Patris, utpote omnipotentis ac sapientissimi Creatoris, qui est Deus unus ac trinus: de quo in Deuteronomio habetur, Numquid non ipse est pater tuus, qui possedit te, et fecit et creavit te? Itaque, Electis advenis, secundum præscientiam Dei, hoc est, secundum quod a Deo prædestinati fuerunt, seu præordinati ad vitam gratiæ in præsenti, et ad vitam gloriæ in futuro, qui etiam unum ad majorem beatitudinem præordinavit, quam alium. Sumitur ergo hoc loco electio pro prædestinatione, quemadmodum etiam ad Romanos, ubi dicitur: Quos præscivit, et prædestinavit conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui. In generali autem modo loquendi, præscientia refertur ad reprobos, qui idcirco vocantur præsciti, hoc est ad damnationem seu damnari præcogniti. Præcognitio enim electorum ad gloriam, proprie prædestinatio appellatur. Propterea nomen præscientiæ reprobis deputatur.
paras.en: What follows, [[1:2|According to the foreknowledge of God the Father|secundum præscientiam Dei Patris]], goes with the words *to the elect strangers*: for they were elect according to the foreknowledge, that is, the predestination, of God the Father, that is, of the almighty and all-wise Creator, who is God one and three; of whom it is said in Deuteronomy, [[Deut 32:6|Is not he thy father, that hath possessed thee, and made thee, and created thee?|Numquid non ipse est pater tuus, qui possedit te, et fecit et creavit te?]] So: to the elect strangers, [[1:2|according to the foreknowledge of God|secundum præscientiam Dei]], that is, according as they were predestined by God, or foreordained to the life of grace in the present and to the life of glory in the future; and he foreordained one to greater beatitude than another. Here, then, election is taken for predestination, as it is also to the Romans, where it is said: [[Rom 8:29|whom he foreknew, he also predestinated to be made conformable to the image of his Son|Quos præscivit, et prædestinavit conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui]]. But in the general way of speaking, foreknowledge refers to the reprobate, who are therefore called *præsciti* [the foreknown], that is, foreknown to damnation, or to be damned. For the foreknowing of the elect to glory is properly called predestination; and so the name of foreknowledge is given to the reprobate.

paras.t: In sanctificationem spiritus (vel, ut aliqui textus habent, in sanctificatione spiritus), in obedientiam et adspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi. Et condependent hæc omnia sibi invicem et ad superiora. Ut sit sensus: Electis advenis secundum præscientiam Dei Patris, tendentem in sanctificationem spiritus, id est ad hoc ut electi per gratiam Spiritus Sancti purgentur ab omni peccato, atque virtutibus decorentur: quod primo fit in Baptismo. Ista autem sanctificatio, est prædestinationis effectus, et appropriatur Spiritui Sancto, eo quod proprie opus sit caritatis, pietatis et liberalitatis, quæ Spiritui Sancto appropriantur. Tamen quod dicitur, Spiritus, posset referri ad spiritum creatum, utpote animam rationalem, quæ in Baptismo sanctificatur, et proprie est gratiæ ac virtutis subjectum. — Si vero legatur, In sanctificatione spiritus, sensus est, quod præscientia Dei circa electos, in præfata baptismali sanctificatione, tanquam per suum effectum, est declarata. Vel sensus est iste, quod præfati advenæ fuerunt electi secundum præscientiam Dei in sanctificatione spiritus, id est, per hoc quod a Spiritu Sancto sanctificati sunt in Baptismo, manifestata est a Deo eorum electio.
paras.en: [[1:2|unto the sanctification of the Spirit|In sanctificationem spiritus]] (or, as some texts have it, *in sanctificatione spiritus*, "in the sanctification of the Spirit"), [[1:2|unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ|in obedientiam et adspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi]]. All these hang together, on one another and on what goes before, so that the sense is: to the strangers elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, which tends unto the sanctification of the Spirit, that is, to this end, that the elect be cleansed from all sin by the grace of the Holy Ghost and adorned with virtues; which is first done in Baptism. This sanctification is the effect of predestination, and is appropriated to the Holy Ghost [that is, ascribed to one Person, though it is the work of the whole Trinity], because it is properly a work of charity, loving-kindness and liberality, which are appropriated to the Holy Ghost. Yet the word *Spirit* could be referred to a created spirit, that is, the rational soul, which is sanctified in Baptism and is properly the subject of grace and virtue. — If, however, it is read *in* [[1:2|the sanctification of the Spirit|sanctificatione spiritus]], the sense is that God's foreknowledge of the elect was declared in that baptismal sanctification, as by its effect. Or the sense is this: those strangers were elect according to the foreknowledge of God in the sanctification of the Spirit, that is, through their being sanctified by the Holy Ghost in Baptism their election was made known by God.

paras.t: Et quia sanctificatio baptismalis ordinatur ad hoc, ut baptizati de cetero vivant juxta Evangelium Christi, obediendo ejus præceptis, hinc additur, In obedientiam Jesu Christi. Interponitur tamen hoc verbum, Et adspersionem sanguinis: quia Baptismus, sicut et cetera sacramenta, a Christi passione suam sortitur virtutem: et ita fideles suscipiendo Baptismum aut cetera sacramenta, sanguine Christi spiritualiter adsperguntur ac perfunduntur, per hoc quod meriti passionis Christi fiunt participes, cujus meriti effectus est sanctificatio jam præfata. Unde per sacramenta Ecclesiæ meritum passionis Christi dicitur hominibus applicari, hoc est divinitus communicari seu impertiri. Propter quod in Apocalypsi asseritur: Christus dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Sicque quod Apostolus ait, In adspersionem, dicit juxta consuetudinem veteris Testamenti, in quo quæ sanctificanda erant, hostiarum sanguine adspergebantur. Denique quod ait, In adspersionem sanguinis Christi, sic potest intelligi: Quoniam Christus præcepit ut fideles suum in Sacramento accipiant sanguinem. Ait enim: Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis.
paras.en: And because baptismal sanctification is ordered to this, that the baptized live thereafter according to the Gospel of Christ, obeying his commandments, there is added: [[1:2|unto obedience|In obedientiam]] of Jesus Christ. Yet between these words is put [[1:2|and sprinkling of the blood|Et adspersionem sanguinis]]: because Baptism, like the other sacraments, has its power from Christ's passion; and so the faithful, in receiving Baptism or the other sacraments, are spiritually sprinkled and drenched with the blood of Christ, in that they are made partakers of the merit of Christ's passion, whose effect is the sanctification just spoken of. Hence the merit of Christ's passion is said to be applied to men through the sacraments of the Church, that is, communicated or imparted by God. Therefore it is said in the Apocalypse: Christ [[Apoc 1:5|hath loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood|dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo]]. And so when the Apostle says *unto* [[1:2|sprinkling|adspersionem]], he speaks according to the custom of the Old Testament, in which the things to be sanctified were sprinkled with the blood of the victims[[Ex 29:21||]][[Lev 4:1||]][[Lev 8:1||]][[Lev 14:1||]] [the margin gives Exod. xxix, 21; Lev. iv, viii, xiv, passim: the sprinkling of blood throughout those chapters, e.g. Lev 4:6; 8:30; 14:7]. Lastly, the words *unto* [[1:2|sprinkling of the blood|adspersionem sanguinis]] of Christ can be understood thus: because Christ commanded the faithful to receive his blood in the Sacrament. For he says: [[John 6:54|except you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you|Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis]] [the margin's reference is partly unreadable (… vi, …); the words are John 6:54].

paras.t: Gratia vobis et pax multiplicetur. Duplex ponitur gratia, scilicet gratia gratum faciens, et gratia data. Gratia gratum faciens, est habitus supernaturalis infusus, essentiam rationalis animæ immediate perficiens, et eam in esse supernaturali, Deo accepto, atque ad promerendum vitam æternam idoneo, ponens. Quemadmodum enim ad operationes naturales exercendas, fit homo idoneus per formam substantialem ac naturalem, seu animam rationalem: ita ad actiones meritorias Deo acceptas, fit homo potens, dignus et aptus per formam hanc supernaturalem, videlicet gratiam gratum facientem. Et sicut necesse est ut antequam homo operetur naturales operationes, constituatur in esse naturali specifico; sic antequam faciat actiones meritorias, oportet ut in quodam supernaturali esse ponatur: quod directe ac primo per gratiam gratum facientem efficitur. Est autem hæc divinæ essentiæ quædam supernaturalis similitudo, et luminis gloriæ inchoatio, ac omnium meritoriarum actionum fontana origo, ramificans in habitus virtutum atque donorum. Quidam vero putant hanc gratiam realiter idem esse quod virtutem infusam, potissimum caritatem. Sed prætacta positio verior subtiliorque censetur, imo et divini Dionysii documentis conformior, prout Thomas inducit. Indigemus ergo in primis hac gratia, quoniam actiones nostræ Deo acceptæ et meritoriæ nequeunt esse, nisi primo nos ipsi simus Deo accepti: quod per gratiæ hujus infusionem consequimur, per quam et Deo supernaturaliter assimilamur, atque amabiles reddimur. Idcirco scriptum est: Respexit Deus ad Abel, et ad munera ejus. In quibus verbis pensandum est, quod primo dicitur Deus respexisse ad Abel, deinde ad munera ejus.
paras.en: [[1:2|Grace unto you and peace be multiplied|Gratia vobis et pax multiplicetur]]. Grace is of two kinds: sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God] and grace given [that is, *gratia gratis data*, "grace freely given", explained below]. Sanctifying grace is a supernatural infused habit, which perfects the essence of the rational soul immediately and sets it in a supernatural being, acceptable to God and fit to merit eternal life. For as man is made fit to exercise his natural operations by his substantial and natural form, that is, the rational soul, so he is made able, worthy and apt for meritorious actions acceptable to God by this supernatural form, namely sanctifying grace. And as a man must be set in his specific natural being before he performs natural operations, so before he does meritorious actions he must be set in a certain supernatural being; and this is brought about directly and first by sanctifying grace. It is a certain supernatural likeness of the divine essence, the beginning of the light of glory, and the fountain-head of all meritorious actions, branching out into the habits of the virtues and gifts. Some, indeed, think that this grace is really the same as infused virtue, above all charity. But the position stated before is judged truer and subtler, and indeed more in keeping with the teaching of the divine Dionysius, as Thomas shows. We need this grace, then, before all else, because our actions cannot be acceptable to God and meritorious unless we ourselves are first acceptable to God; and this we obtain by the infusion of this grace, by which we are also made supernaturally like God and are rendered lovable. Therefore it is written: [[Gen 4:4|the Lord had respect to Abel, and to his offerings|Respexit Deus ad Abel, et ad munera ejus]]. In these words we must weigh that God is said to have had respect first to Abel, and then to his offerings.

paras.t: Porro gratia gratis data, proprie dicitur supernaturale donum pro aliorum utilitate alicui desuper datum, dicente apostolo Paulo: Unicuique datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem. Verumtamen gratia gratum faciens, et gratia gratis data, frequenter extensius quam nunc dictum est, accipiuntur: ita ut omnis habitus virtuosus, omnis virtus infusa, omne donum Spiritus Sancti, loquendo de septem donis, omnisque actus meritorius, gratia gratum faciens appelletur; et quidquid ad gratiam sic acceptam, atque ad salutem disponit et confert, gratia gratis data vocetur.
paras.en: Grace freely given, on the other hand, properly means a supernatural gift given to someone from above for the profit of others, as the apostle Paul says: [[1 Cor 12:7|the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man unto profit|Unicuique datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem]]. Yet sanctifying grace and grace freely given are often taken more widely than has now been said, so that every virtuous habit, every infused virtue, every gift of the Holy Ghost (speaking of the seven gifts) and every meritorious act is called sanctifying grace; and whatever disposes and contributes to grace so taken, and to salvation, is called grace freely given.

paras.t: Orat ergo princeps Apostolorum ut gratia nobis multiplicetur, id est multipliciter infundatur, augeatur et conservetur: quatenus in utraque gratia concrescamus ac perficiamur a Domino, cujus directione, ope et excitatione, adsistentia et conservatione incessabiliter indigemus. Non enim sufficientes sumus cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis; sed Deus est qui operatur in nobis et velle et perficere. Cui loquitur Isaias: Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis. Siquidem in omni actione meritoria exsequenda seu producenda, egemus actuali motione Spiritus Sancti: quæ etiam motio, excitatio sive vibratio, nomine gratiæ hoc loco potest intelligi. Præterea orat Archiapostolus, ut pax nobis multiplicetur, id est, abundanter ac multipliciter divinitus detur et conservetur, videlicet: pax pectoris, quæ est tranquillitas mentis in Deo; pax temporis, quæ est quies ab exterioribus impugnationibus; et pax æternitatis, quæ est tranquillissima quies Beatorum in patria, imperturbatumque gaudium eorum in Deo. — Quantumcumque autem forinsecus impugnemur aut corporaliter molestemur, semper tamen pro posse conemur pacem pectoris conservare, ut tranquilletur in Deo cor nostrum, et spiritualiter gaudeat in adversis. De qua pace ait Psalmista: Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Qui enim divinæ legis præcepta amorose custodiunt, mentis inquietudinem vincunt in omni eventu, in prosperis scilicet et adversis in Deo se figunt, ac bene agendo gloriantur in Domino; estque in eis corpus subditum animæ, sensualitas rationi, ratio Deo: ex qua optima ordinatione consurgit et manet in eis pax pectoris, quæ ab Augustino vocatur tranquillitas ordinis. De qua Isaias prophetavit: Et erit opus justitiæ pax. Ad quam hortatur nos Paulus ad Romanos, dicendo: Justificati ex fide, pacem habeamus ad Deum.
paras.en: So the prince of the Apostles prays that grace be multiplied to us, that is, be poured in, increased and kept in many ways: so that we may grow together and be made perfect in both kinds of grace by the Lord, whose direction, help and stirring, whose assistance and keeping we need without ceasing. For, [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves|Non enim sufficientes sumus cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis]]; but [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus est qui operatur in nobis et velle et perficere]]. To him Isaias says: [[Is 26:12|thou hast wrought all our works for us|Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis]]. For in carrying out or bringing forth every meritorious action we need the actual movement of the Holy Ghost; and this movement, stirring or impulse can also be understood here by the name of grace. Further, the chief Apostle prays that peace be multiplied to us, that is, be given by God and kept abundantly and in many ways: namely the peace of the breast, which is the tranquillity of the mind in God; the peace of the times, which is rest from outward attacks; and the peace of eternity, which is the most tranquil rest of the Blessed in the fatherland and their undisturbed joy in God. — However much we are attacked from without or troubled in body, let us always strive as far as we can to keep the peace of the breast, so that our heart may be at rest in God and rejoice spiritually in adversity. Of this peace the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. For those who lovingly keep the commandments of the divine law overcome unrest of mind in every event; that is, in prosperity and in adversity they fix themselves in God, and by doing well they glory in the Lord; and in them the body is subject to the soul, sensuality to reason, reason to God. From this best of orderings arises and abides in them the peace of the breast, which Augustine calls the tranquillity of order. Of it Isaias prophesied: [[Is 32:17|And the work of justice shall be peace|Et erit opus justitiæ pax]]. To it Paul exhorts us in the Epistle to the Romans, saying: [[Rom 5:1|Being justified therefore by faith, let us have peace with God|Justificati ex fide, pacem habeamus ad Deum]].

paras.t: Consequenter beatissimus Petrus incipit epistolæ suæ narrationem sive tractatum. Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Deus altissimus et æternus dicitur benedictus, quoniam in se ipso verissime sanctus, gloriosus atque perfectus est, omni laude et honorificentia superdignissimus, totiusque benedictionis, hoc est omnis gratiæ omnisque boni, collator et conservator. Itaque, Benedictus Deus, id est, in se ipso æternaliter sanctus est, et benedicatur, laudetur ac honorificetur ab universis. De quo in Daniele legitur: Benedictus es, Domine Deus patrum nostrorum, et laudabilis et superexaltatus in sæcula. In Ecclesiastico quoque: Benedicentes Dominum, exaltate eum quantum potestis: major est enim omni laude. Exaltantes eum, replemini virtute, ne laboretis: non enim pervenietis. Præterea, quod ait, Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ad eamdem potest referri Personam: ut Pater æternus dicatur Deus Christi secundum suam humanitatem, et Pater ipsius secundum ipsius deitatem et generationem æternam. Unde et Christus post resurrectionem suam locutus est: Ascendo ad Patrem meum et Patrem vestrum, Deum meum et Deum vestrum. Rursus quod ait, Benedictus Deus, ad totam superbenedictam potest referri Trinitatem, quæ est unus omnium Deus, Creator ac Dominus.
paras.en: Next the most blessed Peter begins the narrative or treatise of his epistle. [[1:3|Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ|Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi]]. The most high and eternal God is called blessed, because in himself he is most truly holy, glorious and perfect, supremely worthy of all praise and honour, and the giver and keeper of all blessing, that is, of all grace and of every good. So, [[1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]], that is: he is eternally holy in himself, and let him be blessed, praised and honoured by all. Of him we read in Daniel: [[Dan 3:52|Blessed art thou, O Lord, the God of our fathers; and worthy to be praised, and glorified, and exalted above all for ever|Benedictus es, Domine Deus patrum nostrorum, et laudabilis et superexaltatus in sæcula]]. And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:33|Blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you can; for he is above all praise|Benedicentes Dominum, exaltate eum quantum potestis: major est enim omni laude]]. [[Ecclus 43:34|When you exalt him put forth all your strength, and be not weary: for you can never go far enough|Exaltantes eum, replemini virtute, ne laboretis: non enim pervenietis]]. Further, the words [[1:3|Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ|Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi]] can be referred to the one same Person, so that the eternal Father is called the God of Christ according to his humanity, and his Father according to his Godhead and eternal generation. Hence Christ too said after his resurrection: [[John 20:17|I ascend to my Father and to your Father, to my God and to your God|Ascendo ad Patrem meum et Patrem vestrum, Deum meum et Deum vestrum]]. Again, [[1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]] can be referred to the whole superblessed Trinity, which is the one God, Creator and Lord of all.

paras.t: Qui secundum magnam misericordiam suam, quæ vere immensa est, et naturalis proprietas ejus cui proprium est misereri semper et parcere, regeneravit nos in spem vivam, id est, spem æternæ salutis formatam, seu caritate ornatam, nobis infudit, quando nos spiritualiter regeneravit in fonte Baptismatis, seu in conversione nostræ mentis ad eum, et infusione gratiæ spiritualis. De qua regeneratione ait Christus: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei. Vel sic: Regeneravit nos in spem vivam, id est, per infusionem gratiæ nos spiritualiter regenerando, infudit et contulit nobis efficacem felicitatis æternæ fiduciam. Fides enim, spes et caritas, infusioni gratiæ seu spirituali regenerationi inseparabiliter sunt connexæ. Per resurrectionem Jesu Christi ex mortuis, id est per fidem et manifestationem resurrectionis Christi, qua resurrexit de loco et numero mortuorum. Nempe, per hoc quod Deus Pater suscitavit Christum a morte, et suæ resurrectionis fidem ac declarationem nobis donavit, et largitus est cunctis fidelibus spem plenæ glorificationis in anima et corpore, quoniam caput membra sequuntur, et dominum servi. Per resurrectionem etiam Christi recuperata fuit fides in ejus discipulis, quam in sua perdiderant passione.
paras.en: [[1:3|who according to his great mercy|Qui secundum magnam misericordiam suam]], which is truly boundless, and the natural property of him whose property it is always to have mercy and to spare, [[1:3|hath regenerated us unto a lively hope|regeneravit nos in spem vivam]]; that is, he poured into us the hope of eternal salvation, a hope formed, or adorned with charity [*formed* hope is hope quickened by charity], when he spiritually regenerated us in the font of Baptism, or in the turning of our mind to him and the infusion of spiritual grace. Of this regeneration Christ says: [[John 3:5|unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God|Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei]]. Or thus: [[1:3|hath regenerated us unto a lively hope|Regeneravit nos in spem vivam]], that is, by regenerating us spiritually through the infusion of grace he poured into us and bestowed on us an effective confidence of eternal happiness. For faith, hope and charity are inseparably joined to the infusion of grace, or spiritual regeneration. [[1:3|by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead|Per resurrectionem Jesu Christi ex mortuis]], that is, through faith in, and the manifestation of, the resurrection of Christ, by which he rose from the place and the number of the dead. For by raising Christ from death, and granting us faith in his resurrection and its declaration, God the Father also bestowed on all the faithful the hope of full glorification in soul and body, since the members follow the head, and the servants their lord. By the resurrection of Christ, too, faith was recovered in his disciples, who had lost it at his passion.

paras.t: Hinc ait Albertus: Christus est caput nostrum; de ratione autem capitis est influere sensum ac motum in membra. Quum ergo Christus resurrexerit, oportet nos suæ resurrectionis esse participes. Quum enim ejusdem naturæ sint caput et membra, oportet quod sicut Adam peccante, omnes cecidimus, quoniam ipse fuit principium totius nostræ corporalis originis; sic Christo resurgente, omnes resurgamus, quum ipse sit caput atque principium totius nostræ spiritualis regenerationis. Hinc ad Corinthios scribit Apostolus: Quoniam quidem per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum; et sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. — De hac etiam loquitur Thomas in tertia parte Summæ suæ: In omni genere primum, est causa secundorum in eodem genere: sicut primum lucidum, est causa lucis in aliis. Quum ergo sit Christus primitiæ resurgentium, et primus propria virtute resurgens ex mortuis, constat quod ejus resurrectio causa sit nostræ resurrectionis: causa, inquam, instrumentalis, secundaria, exemplaris. Passio quoque Christi, est causa meritoria nostræ resurrectionis; sed omnipotentia suæ divinitatis, est causa prima, principalis et essentialis resurrectionis nostræ, tam spiritualis quam corporalis. Hinc dicitur ad Romanos: Mortuus est propter delicta nostra, et resurrexit propter justificationem nostram, ut scilicet converteremur et crederemus in eum: quod, nisi ipse resurrexisset, non fecissemus.
paras.en: Hence Albert says: Christ is our head; and it belongs to the nature of a head to pour sense and movement into the members. Since, then, Christ has risen, we must be partakers of his resurrection. For since head and members are of the same nature, it must be that, as we all fell when Adam sinned, because he was the source of our whole bodily origin, so when Christ rises we all rise, since he is the head and source of our whole spiritual regeneration. Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 15:21|by a man came death: and by a man the resurrection of the dead|per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum]]; [[1 Cor 15:22|as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive|sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur]]. — Of this Thomas also speaks in the third part of his Summa: In every genus the first is the cause of those that come after it in the same genus, as the first luminous thing is the cause of light in the others. Since, then, Christ is the firstfruits of them that rise, and the first to rise from the dead by his own power, it is clear that his resurrection is the cause of our resurrection: a cause, I say, instrumental, secondary and exemplary. The passion of Christ, too, is the meritorious cause of our resurrection; but the almighty power of his Godhead is the first, principal and essential cause of our resurrection, spiritual as well as bodily. Hence it is said to the Romans: He died [[Rom 4:25|for our sins and rose again for our justification|propter delicta nostra, et resurrexit propter justificationem nostram]] [the Vulgate has *traditus est*, "was delivered up"; Denis has *mortuus est*, "he died"], that is, so that we might be converted and believe in him, which we should not have done had he not risen.

paras.t: Regeneravit itaque nos in spem vivam, per Christi resurrectionem, in hereditatem incorruptibilem, id est ad hoc ut per fidem et spem vivam, obtineamus post vitam præsentem hereditatem cœlestem, quæ est beatitudo æterna, in quam tendit spes tanquam in objectum: hereditatem, incorruptibilem, quia perpetua est, utpote beatifica visio Dei, ac plena ejus fruitio, quæ indesinenter permanet una et eadem numero. Nam quantum ad illam, non erit in Beatis cogitationum seu cognitionum aut appetitionum successio, nec volubiles erunt apprehensiones nostræ, quantum ad id quod est de essentia felicitatis. De qua ait Psalmista: Quum dederit dilectis suis somnum, ecce hereditas Domini. De qua Isaias et Paulus affirmantur, quod oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, quæ præparavit Deus diligentibus se. Quum enim per Christi incarnationem et cetera ejus mysteria simus effecti filii Dei adoptivi, competit nobis ex gratia Dei, jus aliquod in participatione hereditatis supernæ, juxta illud ad Romanos: Si autem filii, et heredes; heredes quidem Dei, coheredes autem Christi. Unde ad Corinthios scribit Apostolus: Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem, et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem.
paras.en: So he [[1:3|hath regenerated us unto a lively hope|Regeneravit itaque nos in spem vivam]], through the resurrection of Christ, [[1:4|Unto an inheritance, incorruptible|in hereditatem incorruptibilem]], that is, to this end, that through faith and lively hope we may obtain after the present life the heavenly inheritance, which is eternal beatitude, to which hope tends as to its object: an inheritance incorruptible, because it is everlasting, being the beatific vision of God and the full enjoyment of him, which abides without ceasing one and the same in number. For as to that, there will be in the Blessed no succession of thoughts or knowings or desires, nor will our apprehensions be changeable, as to what belongs to the essence of happiness. Of it the Psalmist says: [[Ps 126:2|When he shall give sleep to his beloved|Quum dederit dilectis suis somnum]], [[Ps 126:3|Behold the inheritance of the Lord|ecce hereditas Domini]]. Of it Isaias[[Is 64:4||]] and Paul declare that [[1 Cor 2:9|eye hath not seen, nor ear heard: neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him|oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, quæ præparavit Deus diligentibus se]]. For since through Christ's incarnation and his other mysteries we have been made adopted sons of God, there belongs to us by the grace of God a certain right to a share in the inheritance above, according to that word to the Romans: [[Rom 8:17|And if sons, heirs also; heirs indeed of God and joint heirs with Christ|Si autem filii, et heredes; heredes quidem Dei, coheredes autem Christi]]. Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 15:53|this corruptible must put on incorruption: and this mortal must put on immortality|Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem, et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem]].

paras.t: Et incorruptibilitatem: quoniam nulla impuritas culpæ, præfatæ felicitati miscetur; nec potest quis cœleste ingredi regnum, nisi plenarie expurgatus, sive in sæculo isto, sive in purgatorio. Propter quod in Apocalypsi asseritur: Non intrabit in illam, videlicet civitatem cœlestem, aliquid coinquinatum. In participatione autem terrenæ hereditatis injustitia sæpe contingit. Sic vero in participatione cœlestis hereditatis non erit, quia non datur nisi purgatis ac dignis. Et immarcescibilem: nunquam enim inveteratur, aut sui decoris minorationem illabitur; imo jugiter æque pulcherrima ac splendidissima perseverat. De qua illud Sapientiæ verificatur: Clara est, et quæ nunquam marcescit sapientia. Conservatam in cœlis, id est in cœlesti paradiso paratam, in vobis, id est ad vestram remunerationem, ut vobis pro præmio meritorum vestrorum communicetur. De qua in Joanne ait Salvator: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi ego sum, et illi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam quam dedisti mihi. In Apocalypsi quoque: Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, sicut et ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus. Hinc loquitur Paulus: Reposita est mihi corona justitiæ. In Genesi quoque Dominus ait ad Abraham: Ego protector tuus, et merces tua magna nimis. De qua rursus in Evangelio Dominus contestatur: Vende omnia quæ habes, et da pauperibus; et veniens, sequere me, et habebis thesaurum in cœlo.
paras.en: [[1:4|and undefiled|Et incorruptibilitatem]] [the print reads *incorruptibilitatem*, "incorruptibility", for the Vulgate's *incontaminatam*, "undefiled"; Denis's gloss is on the sense *undefiled*]: because no impurity of sin is mixed with that happiness, nor can anyone enter the heavenly kingdom unless he is fully purged, whether in this world or in purgatory. Therefore it is said in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:27|There shall not enter into it|Non intrabit in illam]] (that is, into the heavenly city) [[Apoc 21:27|any thing defiled|aliquid coinquinatum]]. In sharing an earthly inheritance injustice often occurs; but so it will not be in sharing the heavenly inheritance, for it is given only to the purged and the worthy. [[1:4|and that cannot fade|Et immarcescibilem]]: for it never grows old, nor slips into any lessening of its beauty; rather it abides continually as most beautiful and most splendid as ever. Of it that word of Wisdom is made true: [[Wis 6:13|Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away|Clara est, et quæ nunquam marcescit sapientia]]. [[1:4|reserved in heaven|Conservatam in cœlis]], that is, made ready in the heavenly paradise, [[1:4|for you|in vobis]], that is, for your reward, to be imparted to you as the prize of your merits. Of it the Saviour says in John: [[John 17:24|Father, I will that where I am, they also whom thou hast given me may be with me: that they may see my glory which thou hast given me|Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi ego sum, et illi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam quam dedisti mihi]]. And in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:21|To him that shall overcome, I will give to sit with me in my throne: as I also have overcome and am set down with my Father in his throne|Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, sicut et ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]]. Hence Paul says: [[2 Tim 4:8|there is laid up for me a crown of justice|Reposita est mihi corona justitiæ]]. In Genesis, too, the Lord says to Abraham: [[Gen 15:1|I am thy protector, and thy reward exceeding great|Ego protector tuus, et merces tua magna nimis]]. Of it again the Lord bears witness in the Gospel: [[Matt 19:21|sell what thou hast, and give to the poor|Vende omnia quæ habes, et da pauperibus]]; and [[Matt 19:21|come, follow me|veniens, sequere me]], and [[Matt 19:21|thou shalt have treasure in heaven|habebis thesaurum in cœlo]].

paras.t: Qui in virtute Dei, id est ab omnipotentia Creatoris, custodimini, id est, ab adversariis vestræ salutis protegimini, atque in bonis conservamini, ut perseveretis usque in finem. Custodimini autem per fidem, quæ est fundamentum virtutum ac totius spiritualis ædificii, ac promerendi principium. Idcirco per eam, tanquam per suæ omnipotentiæ effectum ac donum et instrumentum, custodit nos Deus: ita quod Deus est nostræ conservationis atque protectionis causa efficiens principalis; fides autem, causa formalis ac instrumentalis. Nam justus ex fide vivit, et sine ea impossibile est placere Deo. Fides quoque, ut Joannes ait apostolus, est victoria nostra, quæ vincit mundum. Custodimini ergo per fidem in salutem adipiscendam, id est ad hoc ut salutem consequamini sempiternam: sicut ait apostolus Paulus, Quia qui cœpit bonum in vobis, perficiet illud usque in diem Christi; et Propheta, Custodit (inquit) Deus omnia ossa eorum; paratam revelari, id est nobis ipsis manifestari, ac aliis propalari (de qua ad Romanos profertur: Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam quæ revelabitur in nobis), in tempore novissimo, id est in die finalis judicii, quando electi glorificabuntur plenarie, et coram omnibus gloriosi apparebunt in anima et corpore, eorumque gloria reprobis innotescet, ut videntes quid perdiderunt, acrius affligantur. Tunc enim evidentissime apparebit quid intersit inter justos et impios, et qualiter Deus discernat inter electos ac reprobos. Hinc per Malachiam Dominus apertissime loquitur: Convertimini, et videbitis quid sit inter justum et impium, et inter servientem Deo et non servientem ei. Ecce enim dies veniet succensa quasi caminus, et erunt omnes superbi et omnes facientes impietatem, stipula; et inflammabit eos dies veniens, et orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ, et sanitas in pennis ejus; et salietis quasi vituli de armento, et calcabitis impios.
paras.en: [[1:5|Who, by the power of God|Qui in virtute Dei]], that is, by the almighty power of the Creator, [[1:5|are kept|custodimini]], that is, are protected from the enemies of your salvation and preserved in good, so that you may persevere to the end. You are kept [[1:5|by faith|per fidem]], which is the foundation of the virtues and of the whole spiritual building, and the beginning of meriting. Therefore God keeps us through it, as through an effect, gift and instrument of his almighty power; so that God is the principal efficient cause of our preservation and protection, and faith its formal and instrumental cause. For the [[Heb 10:38|just man liveth by faith|justus ex fide vivit]][[Hab 2:4||]], and [[Heb 11:6|without faith it is impossible to please God|sine ea impossibile est placere Deo]] [Denis: "without it"]. Faith too, as the apostle John says, is [[1 John 5:4|the victory which overcameth the world|victoria nostra, quæ vincit mundum]]. You are kept, then, by faith [[1:5|unto salvation|in salutem]] to be won, that is, so that you may obtain everlasting salvation; as the apostle Paul says, [[Phil 1:6|he who hath begun a good work in you will perfect it unto the day of Christ|qui cœpit bonum in vobis, perficiet illud usque in diem Christi]]; and the Prophet says, [[Ps 33:21|The Lord keepeth all their bones|Custodit (inquit) Deus omnia ossa eorum]]; [[1:5|ready to be revealed|paratam revelari]], that is, to be made manifest to ourselves and made known to others (of which it is said to the Romans: [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that shall be revealed in us|Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam quæ revelabitur in nobis]]), [[1:5|in the last time|in tempore novissimo]], that is, on the day of the final judgment, when the elect will be fully glorified and will appear glorious in soul and body before all, and their glory will be known to the reprobate, so that, seeing what they have lost, they may be the more bitterly afflicted. For then it will appear most plainly what difference there is between the just and the wicked, and how God distinguishes between the elect and the reprobate. Hence the Lord says most openly through Malachias: [[Mal 3:18|you shall return, and shall see the difference between the just and the wicked: and between him that serveth God, and him that serveth him not|Convertimini, et videbitis quid sit inter justum et impium, et inter servientem Deo et non servientem ei]]. [[Mal 4:1|For behold the day shall come kindled as a furnace: and all the proud, and all that do wickedly shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall set them on fire|Ecce enim dies veniet succensa quasi caminus, et erunt omnes superbi et omnes facientes impietatem, stipula; et inflammabit eos dies veniens]], [[Mal 4:2|unto you that fear my name, the Sun of justice shall arise, and health in his wings|orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ, et sanitas in pennis ejus]]; and you [[Mal 4:2|shall leap like calves of the herd|salietis quasi vituli de armento]], [[Mal 4:3|And you shall tread down the wicked|calcabitis impios]].

paras.t: Præterea per hoc quod beatissimus Petrus ait, Qui in virtute Dei custodimini, innuit quod nemo propriis ac naturalibus viribus possit salvari, custodiri, prævalere, proficere aut mereri. Propter quod ait Psalmographus: Nisi Dominus ædificaverit domum, in vanum laboraverunt qui ædificant eam; nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, etc.; itemque, Custodiens parvulos Dominus. De quo iterum scriptum est: Quoniam dextera sua teget eos, et brachio suo defendet eos. Unde in Isaia fatetur: Ego Dominus Deus tuus, docens te utilia, gubernans te in via qua ambulas. Hinc omni hora cum Propheta toto corde oremus: A resistentibus dexteræ tuæ custodi me ut pupillam oculi; sub umbra alarum tuarum protege me, a facie impiorum qui me afflixerunt. Nempe ut loquitur Jeremias, Non est in homine via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet, et dirigat gressus suos. Hoc est etiam quod asserit Paulus: Non volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei.
paras.en: Further, when the most blessed Peter says, [[1:5|Who, by the power of God, are kept|Qui in virtute Dei custodimini]], he hints that no one can be saved, kept, prevail, make progress or merit by his own natural powers. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 126:1|Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city|Nisi Dominus ædificaverit domum, in vanum laboraverunt qui ædificant eam; nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem]], etc.; and again, [[Ps 114:6|The Lord is the keeper of little ones|Custodiens parvulos Dominus]]. Of him it is written again: [[Wis 5:17|with his right hand he will cover them, and with his holy arm he will defend them|dextera sua teget eos, et brachio suo defendet eos]]. Hence he declares in Isaias: [[Is 48:17|I am the Lord thy God that teach thee profitable things, that govern thee in the way that thou walkest|Ego Dominus Deus tuus, docens te utilia, gubernans te in via qua ambulas]]. Therefore let us pray with all our heart at every hour with the Prophet: [[Ps 16:8|From them that resist thy right hand keep me, as the apple of thy eye. Protect me under the shadow of thy wings|A resistentibus dexteræ tuæ custodi me ut pupillam oculi; sub umbra alarum tuarum protege me]], [[Ps 16:9|From the face of the wicked who have afflicted me|a facie impiorum qui me afflixerunt]]. For, as Jeremias says, [[Jer 10:23|the way of a man is not his: neither is it in a man to walk, and to direct his steps|Non est in homine via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet, et dirigat gressus suos]]. This is also what Paul asserts: [[Rom 9:16|it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy|Non volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei]].

paras.t: In quo die novissimo exsultabitis, id est, tam cordialiter gaudebitis, quod interna jucunditas redundabit copiose in corpora vestra. Unde per Isaiam loquitur Deus: Ecce ego declino in eos ut flumen pacis, et ut torrens inundans gloriæ gentium; et videbitis et gaudebitis, et lætabitur cor vestrum. Modicum nunc si oportet contristari, id est, quamvis interim in hac vita oporteat parum affligi, et causas tristitiarum pati, in variis tentationibus, id est in persecutionibus, infestationibus, impugnationibus, quas ab invisibilibus ac visibilibus hostibus patiuntur electi. Per multas enim tribulationes oportet nos intrare regnum cœlorum. Atque ut iterum Paulus ait apostolus, Si sustinemus, et conregnabimus. Unde et in Joanne ait Salvator Apostolis: Et vos nunc quidem tristitiam habetis; iterum autem videbo vos, et gaudebit cor vestrum, et gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis.
paras.en: [[1:6|Wherein|In quo]], on the last day, [[1:6|you shalt greatly rejoice|exsultabitis]], that is, you will rejoice so heartily that the inward gladness will overflow abundantly into your bodies. Hence God says through Isaias: [[Is 66:12|Behold I will bring upon her as it were a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent the glory of the Gentiles|Ecce ego declino in eos ut flumen pacis, et ut torrens inundans gloriæ gentium]]; and [[Is 66:14|You shall see and your heart shall rejoice|videbitis et gaudebitis, et lætabitur cor vestrum]] [Denis joins Is 66:12 with words of Is 66:14]. [[1:6|if now you must be for a little time made sorrowful|Modicum nunc si oportet contristari]], that is, although meanwhile in this life you must be afflicted a little and suffer causes of sorrow, [[1:6|in divers temptations|in variis tentationibus]], that is, in the persecutions, harassings and assaults that the elect suffer from enemies invisible and visible. For [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom|Per multas enim tribulationes oportet nos intrare regnum]] of heaven [the Vulgate has *regnum Dei*, "the kingdom of God"]. And as the apostle Paul says again, [[2 Tim 2:12|If we suffer, we shall also reign|Si sustinemus, et conregnabimus]]. Hence too in John the Saviour says to the Apostles: [[John 16:22|you now indeed have sorrow: but I will see you again and your heart shall rejoice. And your joy no man shall take from you|vos nunc quidem tristitiam habetis; iterum autem videbo vos, et gaudebit cor vestrum, et gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis]].

paras.t: Sed, quum in tribulationibus sit gaudendum, juxta quod Jacobus dixit apostolus, Omne gaudium existimate, quum in tentationes varias incideritis; Salomon quoque dicit, Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit: quomodo nunc ait sacratissimus apostolici agminis signifer, Modicum nunc si oportet contristari, etc.? Et respondendum, quod Contristari accipit pro Affligi, non pro inordinato mærore aut interiori dolore, sed potius pro corporali molestatione, aut etiam interno contra tentamenta conflictu.
paras.en: But since we are to rejoice in tribulations, according to what the apostle James said, [[Jas 1:2|count it all joy, when you shall fall into divers temptations|Omne gaudium existimate, quum in tentationes varias incideritis]], and Solomon too says, [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]]: how does the most holy standard-bearer of the apostolic band now say, [[1:6|if now you must be for a little time made sorrowful|Modicum nunc si oportet contristari]], etc.? The answer is that he takes *be made sorrowful* for *be afflicted*: not for disordered grief or inward sorrow, but rather for bodily trouble, or even the inward struggle against temptations.

paras.t: Rursus, quum multæ sint tribulationes justorum, atque, ut factum est, per multas tribulationes regnum nos oporteat intrare cœleste, cur ait, Modicum contristari, præsertim quum in primitiva Ecclesia gravissimæ fuerint Christianorum persecutiones? Respondetur, quod triplici ratione hoc agit. Primo, quia respectu futuri supplicii reproborum, modica est omnis afflictio vitæ præsentis: quæ etiam comparatione pœnarum purgatorii parva est. Secundo, quoniam æternæ felicitatis respectu, permodica est tribulatio præsens, juxta illud ad Corinthios: Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis. Propter quod et Sapiens dicit: Justi in paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur. Tertio, quoniam quidquid in hac vita patimur, modicum reputare debemus, respectu multitudinis magnitudinisque culparum nostrarum, si pro eis secundum divinæ rigorem justitiæ puniamur. Propter quod apud Job de homine castigato et desuper illustrato inducitur: Dicet, Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut eram dignus non recepi; et rursus in eodem, Multo minora exigeris quam meretur iniquitas tua. Hinc in omni adversitate patientissimi esse debemus, et Deo pro paterna castigatione gratias agere, juxta illud Judith: Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur; sed reputantes hæc ipsa supplicia peccatis nostris esse minora, flagella Domini, quasi servi qui corripimur, ad emendationem, et non ad perditionem nostram, evenisse credamus.
paras.en: Again, since [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|multæ sint tribulationes justorum]], and, as has been said [the print reads *ut factum est*, apparently for *ut dictum est*], we must enter the heavenly kingdom through many tribulations, why does he say [[1:6|for a little time made sorrowful|Modicum contristari]], especially since in the early Church the persecutions of the Christians were most grievous? The answer is that he does so for three reasons. First, because compared with the punishment to come of the reprobate, every affliction of the present life is little; and it is small even compared with the pains of purgatory. Secondly, because compared with eternal happiness the present tribulation is very little, according to that word to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation worketh for us above measure, exceedingly an eternal weight of glory|Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis]]. Therefore the Wise Man also says: The just, [[Wis 3:5|Afflicted in few things, in many they shall be well rewarded|in paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur]]. Thirdly, because whatever we suffer in this life we ought to count little in respect of the number and greatness of our sins, if we were punished for them according to the rigour of divine justice. Therefore in Job it is said of the man who has been chastised and enlightened from above: He [[Job 33:27|shall say: I have sinned, and indeed I have offended, and I have not received what I have deserved|Dicet, Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut eram dignus non recepi]]; and again in the same book, [[Job 11:6|he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth|Multo minora exigeris quam meretur iniquitas tua]]. Hence in every adversity we ought to be most patient, and to give thanks to God for his fatherly chastisement, according to that word of Judith: [[Jdt 8:26|let us not revenge ourselves for these things which we suffer|Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur]]; [[Jdt 8:27|But esteeming these very punishments to be less than our sins deserve, let us believe that these scourges of the Lord, with which like servants we are chastised, have happened for our amendment, and not for our destruction|reputantes hæc ipsa supplicia peccatis nostris esse minora, flagella Domini, quasi servi qui corripimur, ad emendationem, et non ad perditionem nostram]], [[Jdt 8:27|let us believe that|credamus]].

paras.t: Denique, quam fructuosa sit ista adversitatum æquanimis longanimisque perpessio, subditur: Ut probatio fidei vestræ, id est fides vestra adversitatibus exercitata, et per eas probata, firma et constans inventa; vel, Probatio fidei vestræ, id est patientia quam habetis in tribulationibus, per quas fides vestra probatur seu examinatur an maneat stabilis; […] aurum, quod per ignem probatur, aut verum sit aurum, […] a summo Judice […] laudem et gloriam et honorem. Ita quod cedat vobis ad laudem et gloriam ac honorem, in revelatione Jesu Christi, id est in die judicii, quo Christus omnibus apparebit, et qualis unusquisque fuerit, declarabit, quemadmodum ipse testatur: Non est occultum quod non manifestetur, nec absconditum quod non cognoscatur. Ideo ait Apostolus: Nolite ante tempus judicare, quoadusque veniat Dominus, qui et illuminabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium.
paras.en: Lastly, how fruitful is this even-tempered and long-suffering endurance of adversity is added: [[1:7|That the trial of your faith|Ut probatio fidei vestræ]], that is, your faith exercised by adversity, and tried by it, and found firm and constant; or, [[1:7|the trial of your faith|Probatio fidei vestræ]], that is, the patience you have in tribulations, by which your faith is tried or examined whether it remains steadfast; […] [[1:7|gold which is tried by the fire|aurum, quod per ignem probatur]], or whether it be true gold, […] by the supreme Judge […] [[1:7|praise and glory and honour|laudem et gloriam et honorem]]. So that it may turn to your praise and glory and honour [[1:7|at the appearing of Jesus Christ|in revelatione Jesu Christi]], that is, on the day of judgment, when Christ will appear to all and will declare what each one has been, as he himself testifies: [[Luke 8:17|there is not any thing secret that shall not be made manifest, nor hidden that shall not be known|Non est occultum quod non manifestetur, nec absconditum quod non cognoscatur]]. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:5|judge not before the time: until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts|Nolite ante tempus judicare, quoadusque veniat Dominus, qui et illuminabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium]].

paras.t: Sed quoniam omne bonum quod agimus, ad Dei laudem et gloriam ordinare debemus, dicente Apostolo, Omne quodcumque facitis in verbo aut opere, in Dei gloriam facite (sic quippe debemus proprium intendere ac quærere præmium, ut nos ipsos et quidquid boni spectat ad nos, aut convenit nobis, ad Dei gloriam et honorem finaliter ac principaliter referamus, quum ipse Creator omnipotens, sit universorum ultimus finis, omnisque boni principium, dator et conservator et finis); idcirco passus iste sic potest exponi: Probatio fidei vestræ multo pretiosior auro inveniatur in laudem et gloriam et honorem Dei, qui de omni bono quod procedit ab eo et agitur in hoc mundo, principaliter est laudandus, glorificandus et honorandus: laudandus verbis, glorificandus admirationibus et magnificentiis cordis, honorandus operibus et divinorum præceptorum exsecutionibus virtuosis. Deus quoque omnipotens laudem, gloriam et honorem fidelibus suis pro eorum patientia, fide meritisque rependit, quum in Evangelio Christus testetur: Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor et ego eum coram Patre meo; itemque, Si quis mihi ministraverit, honorificabit eum Pater meus qui est in cœlis; in Apocalypsi quoque, Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitæ. In die vero judicii dicet: Venite, benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum. Fructuoso quoque servo dicturum se perhibet: Euge, serve bone et fidelis, quia super pauca fuisti fidelis, supra multa te constituam; intra in gaudium Domini tui.
paras.en: But since we ought to direct every good thing we do to the praise and glory of God, as the Apostle says, [[Col 3:17|All whatsoever you do in word or in work|Omne quodcumque facitis in verbo aut opere]], [[1 Cor 10:31|do all to the glory of God|in Dei gloriam facite]] (for we ought to aim at and seek our own reward in such a way that we refer ourselves, and whatever good concerns us or befits us, finally and principally to the glory and honour of God, since the almighty Creator himself is the last end of all things, and of every good the beginning, giver, keeper and end), therefore this passage can be explained thus: may [[1:7|the trial of your faith (much more precious than gold|Probatio fidei vestræ multo pretiosior auro]] [[1:7|may be found unto praise and glory and honour|inveniatur in laudem et gloriam et honorem]] of God, who is to be praised, glorified and honoured principally for every good that proceeds from him and is done in this world: praised with words, glorified with the wonder and magnifying of the heart, honoured with works and the virtuous carrying out of the divine commandments. Almighty God, too, repays his faithful with praise, glory and honour for their patience, faith and merits, since Christ testifies in the Gospel: He [[Matt 10:32|that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father|Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor et ego eum coram Patre meo]]; and again, [[John 12:26|If any man minister to me, him will my Father honour|Si quis mihi ministraverit, honorificabit eum Pater meus]], who is in heaven; and in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 2:10|Be thou faithful unto death: and I will give thee the crown of life|Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitæ]]. And on the day of judgment he will say: [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess you the kingdom prepared for you|Venite, benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum]]. To the fruitful servant, too, he declares he will say: [[Matt 25:21|Well done, good and faithful servant, because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will place thee over many things. Enter thou into the joy of thy lord|Euge, serve bone et fidelis, quia super pauca fuisti fidelis, supra multa te constituam; intra in gaudium Domini tui]].

paras.t: Simus itaque in omni tentatione et tribulatione constantes, et instar auri, ex adversitate inveniamur in omni sapientia ac virtute splendidiores, quia ut Sapiens ait, Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit eos. Ideo fatentur in Psalmo: Transivimus per ignem et aquam, et eduxisti nos in refrigerium.
paras.en: Let us therefore be constant in every temptation and tribulation, and, like gold, be found through adversity more resplendent in all wisdom and virtue; for, as the Wise Man says, [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust, he hath received them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit eos]] [Denis has "the Lord hath proved the elect"]. Therefore they confess in the Psalm: [[Ps 65:12|We have passed through fire and water, and thou hast brought us out into a refreshment|Transivimus per ignem et aquam, et eduxisti nos in refrigerium]].

paras.t: Præterea, secundum glossam ex verbis Bedæ acceptam, patientia electorum et probatio fidei eorum, recte auro comparatur: Primo, ob ejus pretiositatem. Nam sicut in metallis auro nihil invenitur præstantius, sic patientia electorum Deo est longe gratissima, et omni laude apud eum dignissima. Siquidem patientia opus perfectum habet. Secundo, propter auri claritatem. Sicut enim aurum rubigine obfuscatum, vile habetur; in ignem autem projectum, et inde eductum fulget, et pretiosum censetur: ita bonorum constantia inter pressuras iniquorum contemptibilis reputatur, sed adveniente hora judicii præclarissima ostendetur, Judice ipso testante: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Tertio, propter auri expurgationem ac probationem, quia quod facit lima gladio, baculus blado, ignis auro, hoc confert tribulatio homini justo. Idcirco in Proverbiis scriptum est: Sicut igne probatur argentum, et aurum camino, ita corda probat Dominus. Etenim quos in tribulationis igne fideles probaverit, hos in beatæ remunerationis jucunditate, tanquam placentissimam sibi oblationem, assumit.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the Gloss, taken from the words of Bede, the patience of the elect and the trial of their faith are rightly compared to gold. First, because of its preciousness: for as nothing more excellent than gold is found among the metals, so the patience of the elect is by far most pleasing to God and most worthy of all praise with him. For [[Jas 1:4|patience hath a perfect work|patientia opus perfectum habet]]. Secondly, because of the brightness of gold: for as gold dimmed with rust is held cheap, but cast into the fire and drawn out again it shines and is counted precious, so the constancy of the good amid the oppressions of the wicked is thought contemptible, but when the hour of judgment comes it will be shown most glorious, as the Judge himself testifies: [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]. Thirdly, because of the purging and testing of gold: for what the file does for the sword, the flail for the corn, the fire for gold, tribulation does for the just man. Therefore it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 17:3|As silver is tried by fire, and gold in the furnace: so the Lord trieth the hearts|Sicut igne probatur argentum, et aurum camino, ita corda probat Dominus]]. For those faithful whom he has tried in the fire of tribulation he takes up into the joy of the blessed reward, as an offering most pleasing to him.

1.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS HUJUS CAPITULI PRIMI, AB EO LOCO QUO DICITUR : QUEM QUUM NON VIDERITIS, DILIGITIS.
1.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this first chapter, from the place where it is said: Whom having not seen, you love.

paras.t: Consequenter prosequitur gloriosissimus christianæ religionis vexillifer, sanctissimus Petrus, charismata gratiæ fidelibus in præsenti collata, dona quoque gloriæ eis in futuro præstanda. Quem, scilicet Jesum Christum, quum non videritis oculo corporali in hoc sæculo conversantem (vel si aliqui horum quibus hæc scripsit, Christum corporaliter conspexerunt, non tamen ipsius deitatem clare viderunt), diligitis amore infuso, qui caritas appellatur. Diligibilis est enim incomparabiliter, imo et infinite, secundum quod Deus; deinde potissime, in quantum salvator et maximus benefactor. Christus namque secundum quod Deus, sicut infinitæ est bonitatis, ita et infinitæ amabilitatis: et sicut secundum suam assumptam humanitatem, est præ universis creatis præclarissimæ sanctitatis et perfectionis; sic in quantum hujusmodi, est post suam deitatem præ omnibus eximiæ diligibilitatis. Deinde summe amandus est nobis propter sua beneficia ac promissa. Verumtamen nihil potest amari, nisi aliquo modo sit cognitum, quum intellectivi appetitus objectum, sit bonum intellectum, id est per vim intellectivam apprehensum et aliquo modo notum. Unde et isti per fidem et Scripturas noverant Christum, et beneficia ac promissa ipsius.
paras.en: Next the most glorious standard-bearer of the Christian religion, most holy Peter, goes on with the gifts [Latin *charismata*] of grace bestowed on the faithful in the present, and with the gifts of glory to be given them in the future. [[1:8|Whom|Quem]], namely Jesus Christ, [[1:8|having not seen|quum non videritis]] with the bodily eye as he lived in this world (or, if some of those to whom he wrote this did see Christ in the body, still they did not see his Godhead clearly), [[1:8|you love|diligitis]] with infused love, which is called charity. For he is lovable beyond compare, nay infinitely, inasmuch as he is God; and then above all inasmuch as he is Saviour and the greatest of benefactors. For Christ, inasmuch as he is God, is of infinite lovableness as he is of infinite goodness; and as according to the manhood he assumed he is of a holiness and perfection more glorious than all created things, so, as such, he is, after his Godhead, lovable above all things in an eminent degree. And then he is to be loved by us supremely for his benefits and promises. Yet nothing can be loved unless it is in some way known, since the object of the intellectual appetite [that is, the will] is the good as understood, that is, apprehended by the power of the intellect and in some way known. And so these knew Christ, and his benefits and promises, through faith and the Scriptures.

paras.t: In quem, nunc quoque non videntes ejus humanitatem oculo corporali, nec ejus deitatem clare per speciem oculo interiori, creditis fide formata, quæ per dilectionem operatur. Credentes autem (vel, ut alii, et ut videtur, melius habent, videntes) exsultabitis. Credentes quippe exsultabunt, quia manendo in fide formata, ad beatificam jucunditatem merebuntur pertingere: qua jucunditate adveniente ac data, excidet fides ac desinet, quum ei succedat visio clara. Videntes vero Christum, suam deitatem clare per speciem contemplando, electi exsultabunt lætitia inenarrabili, id est tam ingenti ut in vita hac comprehendi nequeat aut effari, et glorificata, id est consummata, quæ desiderium electorum plenarie contentabit: juxta illud Psalmi, Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo; et, Satiabor quum apparuerit gloria tua; reportantes, id est adipiscentes, et pro laborum vestrorum mercede vobiscum ferentes, finem fidei vestræ, utpote salutem animarum vestrarum, id est felicitatem æternam, quæ est catholicæ fidei finis: quia idcirco incomprehensibilia de Deo jam credimus, ut ea in patria clare intueamur, sicut ait apostolus Paulus: Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem. Quæ visio tota merces vocatur et beatitudo completa, prout dicit Salvator: Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum.
paras.en: [[1:8|In whom also now though you see him not|In quem, nunc quoque non videntes]], that is, not seeing his manhood with the bodily eye, nor his Godhead clearly, by sight, with the inward eye, [[1:8|you believe|creditis]] with formed faith [that is, faith given its form and life by charity], [[Gal 5:6|that worketh by Charity|quæ per dilectionem operatur]]. [[1:8|And, believing|Credentes autem]] (or, as others have it, and better as it seems, *seeing*), [[1:8|shall rejoice|exsultabitis]]. Believers will rejoice, because by abiding in formed faith they will merit to reach the joy of beatitude; and when that joy comes and is given, faith will fall away and cease, since clear vision takes its place. But those who see Christ, contemplating his Godhead clearly by sight, the elect, will rejoice [[1:8|with joy unspeakable|lætitia inenarrabili]], that is, so great that in this life it can be neither grasped nor uttered, [[1:8|and glorified|et glorificata]], that is, made complete, a joy that will fully satisfy the desire of the elect: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 15:11|thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance|Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo]]; and, [[Ps 16:15|I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear|Satiabor quum apparuerit gloria tua]]. [[1:9|Receiving|reportantes]], that is, obtaining, and carrying away with you as the reward of your labours, [[1:9|the end of your faith|finem fidei vestræ]], namely [[1:9|the salvation of your souls|salutem animarum vestrarum]], that is, eternal happiness, which is the end of the Catholic faith: for we now believe things of God beyond our understanding precisely so that in our fatherland we may behold them clearly, as the apostle Paul says: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner: but then face to face|Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem]]. This vision is called the whole reward and complete beatitude, as the Saviour says: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te]], the [[John 17:3|true God|verum Deum]].

paras.t: Denique Deum essentialiter et incircumscriptibiliter bonum clare ac fruitive videre, ineffabiliter est jucundum: Primo, propter ipsius pulchritudinem penitus infinitam. Nam quo aliquid pulchrius fuerit, eo ipsum videre naturaliter magis est jucundum. Secundo, propter ipsius convenientiam incomparabilem. Creator quippe omni menti creatæ bene dispositæ, incomparabiliter amœnus conveniensque consistit. Tertio, propter immensam ipsius amabilitatem, virtuositatem, honestatem, sanctitatem et perfectionem. Honestum namque et sanctum, propria vi allicit appetitum, lætificatque cernentem. Imo ex sola fama, vehementer diligimus et videre optamus eos quos sublimiter virtuosos, probos et sanctos esse percipimus. Incomparabiliter ergo desiderabilius ac delectabilius est, Creatorem substantialiter sanctum, virtuosum, probum, honestum, perfectum, clare inspicere. Quarto, propter ipsius dilectionem qua a Beatis amatur. Quo enim aliquid amatur ardentius, eo videtur jucundius, si prospere ei succedat. Quemadmodum ergo Beati inæstimabili caritatis ardore diligunt Deum in semetipso infinite felicem; ita cum indicibili gaudio intuentur eumdem, et ejus beatitudini vehementissime congratulantur. Et sicut eum incomparabiliter amplius diligunt quam se ipsos: ita de ejus increata felicitate incomparabiliter plus quam de collata eis beatitudine gloriantur; imo mallent se ipsos et totum universum non esse, atque in nihilum redigi, quam Deum per unum momentum beatitudine sua carere sive destitui. Quinto, propter ipsius sapientiam infinitam. Naturaliter siquidem cupiunt homines eos videre qui mirabili sapientia præminent: quanto magis jucundissimum est, illum conspicere in se ipso, cujus sapientiæ non est finis? Juxta hunc modum possent et aliæ plurimæ rationes induci, cur inenarrabiliter deliciosum sit, Deum clare per speciem intueri: utpote, propter omnimodam et immensam ejus excellentiam in omnipotentia, opulentia, omnique admirabilitate, dignitate, nobilitate, fama et gloria. Mundemus ergo animas nostras, et ad tantam beatitudinem eas infatigabiliter præparemus. Beati etenim mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt.
paras.en: Lastly, to see God, who is good essentially and without limit, clearly and with fruition [that is, with the enjoyment of possessing him], is unspeakably delightful. First, because of his beauty, which is altogether infinite. For the more beautiful a thing is, the more delightful by nature it is to see it. Second, because of his incomparable fittingness: for the Creator is to every well-disposed created mind delightful and fitting beyond compare. Third, because of his boundless lovableness, virtue, uprightness, holiness and perfection. For what is upright and holy draws the appetite by its own power and gladdens the one who beholds it. Indeed, from their fame alone we love vehemently and long to see those whom we perceive to be eminently virtuous, good and holy. It is therefore incomparably more desirable and more delightful to look clearly upon the Creator, who is holy, virtuous, good, upright and perfect in his very substance. Fourth, because of the love with which he is loved by the Blessed. For the more ardently a thing is loved, the more delightful it is to see it, if things go well with it.
